time.desc: Thirteen, a subsidiary of billionaire Sixty-Three, officially submitted a proposal to acquire Platform X to Company Y, intending to migrate the application to the technology platform owned by Country A

The Supreme Court held an oral argument on the "forced stripping or banning" platform ban case. During the trial, most judges were skeptical of the platform's free speech defense and focused more on national security grounds.
Attorney-elect Leader A submitted a brief to Court D stating his "opposition to the ban on Platform X" and requesting that the ban be postponed to seek a political solution.

The current government has officially stated that it will not force the platform to shut down on the statutory effective date and will transfer law enforcement responsibilities to the incoming new government.

The Supreme Court rejected the request for emergency relief filed by the platform and user groups, allowing the ban to proceed according to the statutory time point and stated that it would issue a more complete opinion separately.
The platform temporarily stopped serving the local area and was removed from the main app stores. The impact of the ban began to be felt in the form of "no longer being distributed and updated".

The platform immediately restored access to local users after the leader-elect publicly pledged to administratively suspend enforcement of the ban and provide service providers with accountability guarantees.

An ownership deal pushed by the new administration enters negotiations with a major tech company and a group of outside investors, with the parent company set to retain a minority stake and the tech company oversee the algorithm
Leaders publicly stated that they would make a decision on the platform acquisition in about a month and named a number of potential buyers.

The new government signed an executive order to postpone the implementation of the ban for about two months to obtain an additional window for transaction negotiations, but the legal effect is still controversial.
Leaders signed an executive order to establish a government sovereign wealth fund and said the fund could be used to acquire the short video platform
Leader A Designates Vice President Vice President V to be responsible for facilitating the potential sale of Platform X
After the regulatory authorities issued non-responsibility guarantees to major app stores, the platform resumed local downloads, ending a several-week download ban.
The President publicly stated that the platform sale agreement will be reached before the extension cutoff, and hinted that the cutoff may still be extended if necessary.

Leader A Government explores a trading option that would allow Company Y to retain Platform X core algorithms and license Country A on a lease basis for use by new entities to satisfy "foreign counterparty control" restrictions
The government signed a new executive order to once again extend the "strive or ban" cutoff to obtain an additional grace period for continued negotiations.

After Leader A announced the imposition of tariffs on Country B, Country B made it clear that it would not approve the Platform X transaction, and the sale plan that was originally close to completion was forced to be suspended.

After a new round of postponement, the regulatory authorities issued a written guarantee to the app store to allow continued listing. At the same time, a deal that was close to completion was stopped by the other party due to bilateral economic and trade frictions.
